en: The First Chapter: On Concentration. Now begins the instruction on yoga. 1.1.
Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. //1.2//
Then there is the establishment of the seer in his own true nature. //1.3//
In other cases, there is conformity with the mental modifications. //1.4//
The fivefold fluctuations are either afflicted or unafflicted. (1.5)
Valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory. //1.6//
Perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition. 1.7.
Error is false knowledge, which is not established in the nature of that [object]. //1.8//
Conceptual construction (vikalpa) is that which follows upon verbal knowledge and is devoid of a real object. //1.9//
Sleep is a mental modification whose object is the notion of non-existence. //1.10//
Memory is the non-forgetting of an experienced object. //1.11//
Its cessation is achieved through practice and dispassion. (1.12)
In that regard, effort toward stability is practice (abhyāsa). 1.13.
But that [wholesome root], when practiced with long duration, without interruption, and with reverence, becomes firm ground. 1.14.
Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the consciousness of mastery in one who is free from thirst for objects seen or heard of in tradition. //15//
Beyond that is dispassion toward the gunas, arising from the discernment of the Puruṣa. //1.16//

Cognitive concentration (*samprajñāta-samādhi*) is so called because it follows the forms of applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the sense of self (*asmitā*). //1.17//
The other [samādhi] is preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation and consists of residual latent impressions alone. (1.18)
Existence is the condition for those who are dissolved in the disembodied state or in primordial nature. //1.19//
For others, [the practice] is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. //1.20//
It is near for those with intense spiritual urgency. //1.21//
There is a further distinction [of the paths] due to their being weak, medium, and intense. //1.22//
Or [concentration is attained] through devotion to the Lord. //1.23//
The Lord is a distinct Puruṣa, untouched by the latent impressions of afflictions, actions, and their fruitions. 1.24.
In that [state], there exists the unsurpassed seed of omniscience. //1.25//
He is also the teacher of the ancients, because he is not limited by time. //1.26//
The syllable Om is its designator. 1.27.
The repetition of that [mantra] and the contemplation of its meaning. //1.28//
From that, there arises the realization of the inward-turned consciousness as well as the absence of obstacles. //1.29//

Disease, languor, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, lack of dispassion, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage [of meditation], and instability—these are the distractions of the mind. They are the obstacles. (1.30)
Suffering, mental distress, trembling of the limbs, and inhalation and exhalation are co-existent with distraction. //1.31//
For the purpose of preventing that, there is the practice of a single principle (tattva). //1.32//

The clarification of the mind through the cultivation of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, directed toward the objects of happiness, suffering, merit, and demerit. //1.33//
Or [prāṇāyāma is accomplished] by means of the exhalation and retention of the breath. 1.34.
Or, when an activity of the mind directed toward an object has arisen, it serves as a means for stabilizing the mind. //1.35//
Or it is free from sorrow, or luminous. 1.36.
Or the mind has as its object that which is free from passion. //1.37//
Or it has as its object the cognition of dream or sleep. //1.38//
Or [it arises] from meditation on whatever is desired. //1.39//
His mastery extends from the smallest atom to the greatest magnitude. //1.40//
For one whose fluctuations have ceased,

there occurs a meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) characterized by the identification with the object, the instrument of perception, and the perceiver— whether they reside in those [objects] or are colored by them— just as in the case of a noble gem. (1.41)
Therein, the meditative attainment mixed with conceptual constructions of word, object, and knowledge is "with reasoning" (savitarka). //1.42//
When there is purity of mindfulness, the [meditative concentration] in which the object alone appears as if devoid of its own form is "without discursive thought" (nirvitarka). 1.43.
By this very [sūtra], the subtle-objected [samādhis] with deliberation (savicārā) and without deliberation (nirvicārā) are also explained. //1.44//
And the state of having a subtle object culminates in the unmanifest (aliṅga). //1.45//
These very [attainments] constitute seeded concentration (sabījaḥ samādhiḥ). // 1.46 //
When there is mastery over the state free from subtle reflection, there is inner clarity. //1.47//
In that state, wisdom is truth-bearing. //1.48//
[Direct perception] has an object different from those of the wisdoms derived from hearing and inference, because its object is the particular (viśeṣa). //1.49//
The impression produced by that [meditative concentration] obstructs other impressions. //1.50//
When that too is ceased, because of the cessation of everything, there is seedless samādhi. //1.51//
[Thus ends the first chapter, the Samādhi-pāda, in the Yoga-sūtra composed by Patañjali. The second chapter: Sādhana-pāda.
Austerity (tapas), self-study (svādhyāya), and devotion to the Lord (īśvara-praṇidhāna) constitute the yoga of action (kriyā-yoga). //2.1//
The purpose [of the path] is the cultivation of meditative concentration and the attenuation of the afflictions. //2.2//
Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the afflictions. (2.3)
Ignorance is the field for the subsequent [afflictions], whether they be dormant, attenuated, interrupted, or active. //2.4//
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in that which is impermanent, impure, suffering, and non-self. (2.5)
Asmitā (the sense of "I-am-ness") is the apparent identity between the power of vision and the power of seeing. 2.6.
Attachment is that which lies latent within pleasure. 2.7.
Hatred is that which lies latent within suffering. (2.8)
The innate clinging to existence, which flows by its own inherent force, persists even in the wise man, being so deeply rooted. //2.9//
These subtle [afflictions] are to be abandoned by means of re-absorption. //2.10//
Their fluctuations are to be abandoned by means of meditative absorption (dhyāna). //2.11//
The latent deposit of karma has its root in the afflictions; it is to be experienced in either the present or a future birth. //2.12//
When the root exists, its maturation consists of birth, lifespan, and experience. //2.13//
These have joy and suffering as their fruits, because they have merit and demerit as their causes. //2.14//

Because of the sufferings of transformation, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*, everything is indeed suffering for the discerning person. (2.15)
That which is to be abandoned is future suffering. //2.16//
The conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of that which is to be abandoned. //2.17//

The object of perception (dṛśya), which consists of the elements and the sense organs, has the nature of illumination, activity, and inertia, and exists for the purpose of experience and liberation. 2.18.
The specific, the non-specific, the subtle indicator, and the mere indicator are the stages of the qualities. //2.19//
The seer is pure consciousness alone; though pure, he observes the mental modifications. //2.20//
The very nature of the object of perception is for that purpose alone. //2.21//
Even though it has perished for one who has attained his goal, it is not lost, because it is common to others as well. //2.22//
Conjunction is the cause for the perception of the essential natures of both the self and its master (the Lord). (2.23)
Its cause is ignorance (avidyā). //2.24//
Due to the absence of that [ignorance], there is the absence of conjunction; this is liberation (hāna). That is the isolation (kaivalya) of the Seer. //2.25//
Discriminative discernment, when undisturbed, is the means to liberation. //2.26//
His wisdom is the sevenfold ultimate stage. //2.27//
From the practice of the limbs of yoga, when impurity is destroyed, there is the illumination of knowledge, leading to discriminative discernment. (2.28)
Yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi are the eight limbs. 2.29.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the restraints (yamas). 2.30.
Unrestricted by caste, place, time, or occasion; universal in scope—this is the Great Vow. 2.31.
Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (niyamas). //2.32//
When discursive thought causes affliction, one should cultivate its antidote. //2.33//

For thoughts such as violence, when performed, caused to be performed, or approved; preceded by greed, anger, or delusion; and being mild, moderate, or intense, result in endless suffering and ignorance—this is the cultivation of the counteragent. (2.34)
When non-violence is firmly established, enmity ceases in his presence. (2.35)
When truth is firmly established, there is the attainment of the fruits of action. //2.36//
When non-stealing is firmly established, all jewels present themselves. //2.37//
Upon the foundation of celibacy, there is the attainment of vigor. //2.38//
When non-possessiveness is firmly established, there arises a thorough understanding of the nature of one's births. //2.39//
From purity comes disgust for one's own body and non-association with others. //2.40//
Purity of being, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery over the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self. //2.41//
From contentment comes the unsurpassed attainment of happiness. //2.42//
The perfection of the sense of touch results from the destruction of impurities through austerity. //2.43//
From the private recitation of sacred texts comes communion with one's chosen deity. 2.44.
Success in samādhi comes from devotion to the Lord. 2.45.
Posture is that which is firm and pleasant. 2.46.
[Posture is attained] through the relaxation of effort and through infinite meditative absorption. (2.47)
From that follows non-affliction by the pairs of opposites. 2.48.
When that [posture] is present, the cessation of the flow of inhalation and exhalation is breath control (prāṇāyāma). //2.49//
The flow of the breath, whether external or internal, which is regulated by place, time, and number, becomes long and subtle. (2.50)
The fourth [type of breath restraint] is that which projects the internal and external objects. //2.51//
Thereupon, the veil over the light is destroyed. //2.52//
And there is fitness of the mind for the concentrations (dhāraṇās). //2.53//
Pratyāhāra (withdrawal) is the imitation by the senses of the mind's own nature when they are not in contact with their respective objects. //2.54//
Thereafter, there is supreme mastery over the senses. //2.55//
[Thus ends the second chapter, the Sādhanapāda, in the Yoga-sūtra composed by Patañjali.
The third chapter is the Vibhūtipāda.
Binding the mind to a place is *dhāraṇā* (concentration). //3.1//
In that regard, meditation is the one-pointedness of the mind upon an object. //3.2//
That very [state] in which there is the appearance of the object alone, as if devoid of its own nature, is meditative absorption (samādhi). //3.3//
The three together constitute *saṃyama*. //3.4//
From its victory arises the light of wisdom. //3.5//
Its application is to the stages (bhūmis). //3.6//
The triad [of body, speech, and mind] is more internal than the preceding ones. //3.7//
Even that is external to the seedless [samādhi]. //3.8//

The transformation of cessation is the sequence of moments of cessation, occurring through the suppression of the latent impressions of emergence and the manifestation of the latent impressions of cessation. (3.9)
Its flow becomes tranquil through mental cultivation. //3.10//
The transformation of the mind through concentration consists in the disappearance of its tendency toward all objects and the emergence of one-pointedness. //3.11//
Furthermore: "The transformation of the one-pointedness of the mind consists of the subsided and the arisen being identical in their causal basis. (3.12)
By this, the transformations of property (*dharma*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and state (*avasthā*) regarding the elements (*bhūta*) and the sense organs (*indriya*) have been explained. //3.13//
The substratum (dharmin) conforms to attributes (dharmas) that are quiescent, arisen, or indeterminable. //3.14//
The difference in sequence is the cause for the difference in transformation. //3.15//
Through saṃyama on the three transformations, there is knowledge of the past and the future. //3.16//
There is a confusion of word, object, and idea due to their mutual superimposition. Through *saṃyama* upon their distinction, there arises knowledge of the cries of all living beings. (3.17)
Through the direct realization of the formative forces (saṃskāra), there arises knowledge of previous births. //3.18//
The knowledge of others' minds is the result of [the perfection of] concentration. //3.19//
And that [unconditioned] is not possessed of an object, because it has not become an object [of cognition]. //3.20//
By restraining the body and form, the power of being perceived by them is suppressed; through the non-connection with the light of the eyes, there is invisibility. //3.21//

Karma is of two kinds: that which is subject to external influence (sopakrama) and that which is not subject to external influence (nirupakrama). Through *saṃyama* upon these, there arises knowledge of the end of life;
or [this knowledge comes] from the signs of death (*ariṣṭas*). (3.22)
The powers [are cultivated] in relation to loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables]. //3.23//
Among the powers, there are the elephant-power and so forth. //3.24//
Through the application of the light of the outgoing breath, there arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the remote. //3.25//
Knowledge of the worlds [is attained] through *saṃyama* on the sun. (3.26)
In the moon, there is the knowledge of the array of stars. //3.27//
From the fixed star, there is knowledge of its motion. //3.28//
At the navel-cakra is the knowledge of the array of bodies. //3.29//
In the throat-pit, there is the cessation of hunger and thirst. //3.30//
Stability in the *kūrma* channel. // 3.31 //
When the light at the crown of the head is perceived, there is the vision of the perfected ones (siddhas). //3.32//
Or, by means of intuition, everything [is known]. 3.33.
In the heart, there is the consciousness of the mind. //3.34//

Experience is the non-distinction between the cognitions of the sattva and the puruṣa, which are absolutely unmixed; because it exists for the sake of another, through saṃyama upon one's own purpose, there arises knowledge of the puruṣa. (3.35)
From that, there arise intuitive insight, supernormal hearing, perception of touch, vision, the sense of taste, and knowledge of others' thoughts. (3.36)
These are obstacles to concentration; they are accomplishments when one has emerged from it. 3.37.
Through the loosening of the cause of bondage and through the awareness of the movement of the mind, there occurs the entry of the mind into another body. //3.38//
From mastery over the *udāna* breath, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and the like, as well as the power of upward departure. //3.39//
From the mastery of the *samāna* [vital energy], there is the arising of light. //3.40//
Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the ear and space, divine hearing arises. (3.41)
By *saṃyama* on the connection between the body and space, and through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) on lightness like that of cotton, one attains the power of traveling through space. //3.42//
The external non-conceptualized state is the Great Videha; from that follows the destruction of the veil of light. //3.43//
Through saṃyama upon the gross form, its own nature, its subtle essence, its inherence, and its purposefulness, mastery over the elements is attained. 3.44.
From that, there arises the manifestation of the [eight siddhis] beginning with *aṇimā*, the perfection of the body, and non-obstruction by their properties. //3.45//
The perfection of the body consists of beauty of form, grace, strength, and adamantine firmness. //3.46//
Through *saṃyama* on the essential nature of the senses as grasping, their egoism, their continuity, and their purposefulness, mastery over the senses is attained. (3.47)
From that, there arise: speed of mind, the power of assuming various forms, and mastery over the primary constituents (pradhāna). //3.48//
For one who possesses the mere discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there is sovereignty over all states of being and omniscience. //3.49//
From that dispassion as well, upon the destruction of the seeds of defects, there is isolation (kaivalya). //3.50//
Upon being invited by those who dwell in the higher realms, one should avoid attachment and pride, lest there be the undesirable consequence of returning once more. (3.51)
Through *saṃyama* on the moments and their sequence, knowledge born of discrimination arises. (3.52)
Because difference is not delimited by genus, characteristic marks, or location, the cognition [of difference] arises from those [two] which are otherwise equal. //3.53//
The knowledge born of discrimination is saving, has all things as its object, has everything as its object in every way, and is non-sequential. //3.54//
When there is equality of purity between the sattva and the puruṣa, there is isolation (kaivalya). [YS 3.55]
[Thus ends the third chapter, the Chapter on Supernatural Powers, in the Yoga Sūtras composed by Patañjali.
The Fourth Chapter: The Chapter on Isolation.
Siddhis (accomplishments) are born of birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and samādhi. 4.1.
The transformation into another species occurs through the influx of primordial matter (prakṛti). //4.2//
The efficient cause (nimitta) is not the motivator of the primal natures (prakṛti); rather, it serves to break through their obstruction, like a farmer [who irrigates a field]. //4.3//
The minds of transformation arise from the mere sense of "I-am-ness. (4.4)
The single mind is the motivator for the various activities of many [beings]. (4.5)
Among those, that which is born of meditative absorption (dhyāna) is without residue (anāśaya). //4.6//
The karma of the yogi is neither white nor black; for others, it is of three kinds. //4.7//
Consequently, there is the manifestation only of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are conducive to that specific fruition. //4.8//
There is also immediate succession even for those [impressions] separated by birth, place, and time, because memory and latent impressions (saṃskāra) possess a single form. //4.9//
And their beginninglessness is due to the eternity of the aspiration. (4.10)
Because these are subsumed by way of cause, fruit, basis, and object, in their absence, those [defilements] are absent. //4.11//
The past and the future exist in their own nature, due to the distinction of the time-periods (adhvan) of phenomena (dharma). //4.12//
These manifest and subtle [objects] consist of the gunas. //4.13//
The reality of an object consists in the unity of its transformation. //4.14//
Since the mind differs even when the object is the same, the paths of the two are distinct. //4.15//
And an object is not dependent upon a single mind; if that [mind] were non-existent, what would that object be at that time? //4.16//
Because the mind depends upon the coloring by that [object], an entity is known or unknown. //4.17//
The fluctuations of the mind are always known, because its master, the Puruṣa, is unchanging. //4.18//
That [consciousness] does not have itself as its own appearance, because it is an object of perception. //4.19//
And at one time, there is no determination of both. //4.20//
If one cognition were perceived by another cognition, there would be an infinite regress of cognitions, as well as a confusion of memories. //4.21//
To cite [an example] for the sake of non-transition: when there is an attainment of that aspect, there is the self-awareness of one's own cognition. //4.22//
The mind, colored by the seer and the seen, has all things as its object. //4.23//
Even though it is variegated by incalculable latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it exists for the sake of others, because it acts in combination. //4.24//
For one who perceives the distinction, there is the cessation of the cultivation of the sense of self-existence. [4.25]
Then the mind is inclined toward discernment and gravitates toward isolation. //4.26//
In the intervals between these, other cognitions arise from latent dispositions. //4.27//
Furthermore, their abandonment is said to be like that of the afflictions. //4.28//

For one who is not even attached to discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), there arises, through the complete manifestation of discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*), the *dharmamegha* samādhi. (4.29)
From that follows the cessation of afflictions and karma. //4.30//
Then, because the knowledge that is free from all stains of obscuration is infinite, the knowable is small. //4.31//
Then, for those who have achieved their purpose, there is the completion of the sequence of the transformation of the guṇas. [4.32]
Succession is the counter-positive of the moment, to be grasped by the final limit of transformation. //4.33//
Isolation is the re-absorption of the guṇas when they are devoid of the purposes of the puruṣa, or it is the power of consciousness established in its own nature. (YS 4.34)
[Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Chapter on Isolation, in the Yoga Sūtras composed by Patañjali.
[Thus end the Pātañjala Yoga Sūtras. 1. Afflicted and non-afflicted [citta].
2. *sa* is omitted in the *Vivaraṇa*. These two words may have originally been part of the *Bhāṣya*.
3. *kālādaranai* (KSS); *tkārase* (KSS). 4. *sa* appears at the beginning in the *Vivaraṇa* edition; however, in the KSS edition, *sa* appears at the beginning without brackets. Nevertheless,
Note: The transitional statement (pātanikā) is "This is He. The sūtra is: "He is the teacher even of the ancients, because he is not limited by time" (Vā.
5). [This concludes] the Vivaraṇa on the Bhāṣya.
6. *bhyāṃ* [is used] for the sake of generality (KSS.
7). 7. The word *iti* is not used at the end, as it is used in the case of the final sūtras of the third and fourth pādas.
8. The colophons at the end of the pādas vary considerably in the editions; the manuscripts must...
These should be consulted to determine the original forms of such colophons; they have been supplied here by the editor. 9. *śāḥ pañca kle*—Vidyāsāgara.
10. *nujanmā*—Vivaraṇa.
The *Vivaraṇa* commentary, which also records the reading accepted above, [states]: "nujanmā. 11. The *Vivaraṇa* commentary, which also records the reading accepted above, [states]: "nujanmā."
12. *Trā-liṅga-vivaraṇa*.
13. *Rvāṇa-vivaraṇa*. 14. *Satyamaste-vidyāsāgara*.
15. These [verses] are additionally placed at the beginning in the KSS.
16. *kāgratendri* in the KSS; it is *ekāgratā*, not *aikāgrya*.
is used in 3.11–12, but [as for] the Bhāṣya and Vivaraṇa...
And Vā. has *aikāgrya* here.
17. *ttamasu*: that is, a compound according to Vidyāsāgara;
the Bhāṣya does not indicate how it read the sūtra.
18. *nāntya-* (KSS). 19. *sa tu* appears as an addition at the beginning in KSS;
however, both the *Vivaraṇa* and *Vārttika* clearly indicate that *sa tu* is not part of the sūtra for them.
20. His [name] was Sva-Vidyāsāgara; however, the Bhāṣya and other texts clearly favor the reading as a compound.
21. Therein, the first two words are omitted in the KSS edition; the Vivaraṇa edition reads *pu*.
22. KSS reads *na tat*; the Vivaraṇa reads *ca sā*. 23. KSS reads *śeṣād bho*.
24. *rārthāt* [is] *Vivaraṇa*; *rārthānyasvā* [is] *KSS*. *svārthe saṃ* could have been the reading of the *Vivaraṇa* author.
25. *jayāt* [is] *prajva* [in] *KSS*. 26. *javitvaṃ* [is] *Vidyāsāgara*.
Jhajjar, KSS. Is *jāvatvam* in the *Vivaraṇa* an attempt to eliminate a grammatically difficult *matvarthīya* suffix?
27. *Pama Vivaraṇa*.
28. *iti* is omitted in Jhajjar and KSS; *itiḥ* at the conclusion of the sūtra according to Vā.
29. The doubling [of the consonant] occurs in the āśis according to KSS.
30. *Viviktaḥ* (Vivaraṇa, KSS. 31.
*pekṣitvāt*, Vidyāsāgara, Jhajjar)
KSS. Is *pekṣatvāt* in the *Vivaraṇa* an attempt to eliminate a grammatically problematic *matvarthīya* suffix?
32. *nābhiś* ci—Vidyāsāgara, Jhajjar.
The Bhāṣya in the KSS edition could also have been read thus.
33. *nāni* Vivaraṇa, KSS;
34. *kramasa* Vidyāsāgara.
Jhajjar, KSS.
The reading of Vā. cannot be determined. 35. śakteḥ KSS.
36. The word "iti" in the Sūtra [indicates] the completion of the treatise (Vā.).
